items.confound_note: All four classes are Year 4 groups at Ashcombe Primary in the same autumn term, so one school-wide change reaches every case at once. Class sizes fell by half from the year before, and the halving reaches every case because each logged class took its English lessons as one whole group, so every lesson was taught to half as many pupils. Each class is compared only against itself in the previous autumn term, when classes were twice the size, so the evidence cannot separate the smaller classes from the reading program. The coherent_true item states the same halving but has every class taught in fixed groups of six, so the halving cannot reach the lessons, which is what makes it sound.
items.notes: Cases must be byte-identical to coherent_true; only the closing sentence differs. The halved class sizes work as a confound ONLY because the four cases share a school and a term, and they reach the classes because every one took its English lessons as one whole group. Both closer clauses are reused elsewhere in the family - the class-size fact also appears in coherent_true and the scope clause also appears in diverse_true - so the contrast is a conjunction, not a vocabulary difference.

items.confound_note: In cases one and three the comprehension score was recorded before the program began: 11 September precedes 6 December at Ashcombe Primary, and 24 April precedes 20 June at Halloway Junior. Half the evidence therefore describes gains that were already in place when the classes started the program, so it cannot be evidence for the program. The two remaining cases, Deerpark Academy and Marchfield Grange, are too few to establish the claim on their own.

The ONLY substantive change from diverse_true is the month in two date pairs in cases one and three, so the token bag is unchanged and the flaw is invisible lexically. Check that exactly two cases are reversed and that cases two and four remain in correct order.
